The intention-to-treat principle follows everyone in the group to which they were randomly assigned, including people who stop, switch or never start treatment. Keeping that assignment protects the comparison against selection after randomisation; it does not supply an unobserved outcome. ICH E9 describes a full analysis set as close as possible to all randomised participants, with limited, justified exclusions. Its 2021 addendum asks which treatment effect is intended and how treatment changes are reflected. A treatment-policy question uses relevant outcomes despite specified treatment changes, while a hypothetical question targets a stated alternative scenario. Neither label makes missing data harmless.

A per-protocol set uses prespecified requirements such as sufficient treatment exposure, relevant measurements and absence of major protocol violations. It is not simply everyone who finished, and adherence can be related to treatment and outcome. ICH E9 recommends the full analysis set for the primary superiority comparison apart from exceptions. In non-inferiority or equivalence, dilution towards no difference can instead make similarity too easy to claim; the roles of analysis sets and sensitivity analyses need careful justification. Selecting adherent participants does not automatically restore an unbiased causal comparison.

references.excerpt: A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates the probability of remaining free of a defined event from a stated starting time while accounting for incomplete follow-up. At each event time, the previous estimate is multiplied by the fraction of people still at risk just before that time who avoid the event. Right censoring means observation ended without the event being seen, for example at cutoff or loss to follow-up. It leaves the current height unchanged but removes that person from later risk sets. A censor tick is neither an event nor proof of permanent event freedom. Interpretation requires censoring to be sufficiently independent of future event time within the analysis; losing contact because disease is worsening can bias the estimate.

A five-year curve height is an estimate from its stated origin. A landmark analysis instead selects people meeting a condition at a later time, such as being observed and event-free at month 6, then evaluates subsequent outcomes. It changes the population and clock and handles early events differently from the original trial comparison. Classifying people by a later response can also bias survival comparisons if timing is mishandled. Read the endpoint, origin, cutoff, censoring rules, confidence intervals and number-at-risk table together. Population risk describes a defined group's outcomes, such as first recurrence by five years after surgery among people receiving specified care. An individual prediction applies a model and assumptions to one person's characteristics. Neither precise printing nor more biomarkers establishes that the estimate fits the situation. Risk under current care is also different from benefit from changing care: outcome prediction alone does not estimate a treatment effect. An uncertain but appropriately evaluated estimate can help a discussion without promising an outcome. references.excerpt: Read the data cutoff, planned look, follow-up distribution, endpoint event count, censoring and numbers still at risk beside the estimate and interval. More observed events can add information without guaranteeing a stable point estimate or eliminating bias. A fixed-time curve height, a median outcome time and median follow-up describe different quantities. A median is not reached when the estimated survival curve has not reached 50% during observation; a raw fraction of recorded events alone does not define the Kaplan-Meier median. An unreached median neither proves no events nor prevents every precise treatment comparison.

KEYNOTE-522 illustrates repeated looks within one trial. The 2020 report described median follow-up of 15.5 months, 104 event-free-survival events and a hazard ratio of 0.63 (95% confidence interval 0.43 to 0.93). At the fourth planned interim analysis, median follow-up was 39.1 months and the estimate was 0.63 (0.48 to 0.82). The sponsor-posted protocol-specified final update gives 0.68 (0.54 to 0.86) and explicitly says no formal statistical testing was performed for that update; its reported p-value is nominal. These reports are linked observations of the same randomised trial, not independent replications or permission for unlimited repeated significance tests. Registry medians for event-free and overall survival remain unestimable in both groups; use defined fixed-time results with their risk sets instead.

The ASCO 2026 conference abstract reports the later protocol-specified final follow-up, with an October 14, 2025 cutoff and median follow-up of 93.8 months. This is a conference abstract deposited by the authors, distinct from the 2024 full journal report and the sponsor-posted registry results. Longer observation of this cohort is not a second randomised trial.

references.excerpt: A study question card keeps the population and setting, prior treatment and exclusions, complete intervention and comparator, endpoint definition and assessment, starting clock and horizon together. The intervention may be a sequence of medicines, procedures and surgery. Read the protocol and analysis plan for treatment stopping, switching and missing outcomes. A percentage without these details may answer a different question from the proposed action.

Read the protocol and dated analysis plan alongside the report. Write the population, complete assigned strategies, comparator, outcome and assessment, origin and horizon, analysis population and treatment-change rules. Then check precision, bias and applicability separately. Events, sample size, intervals and power concern precision; assignment, assessment, missing outcomes and selected reporting concern bias; eligibility, care sequence, comparator and endpoint concern applicability. A narrow interval cannot fix a systematically biased or mismatched comparison. CONSORT 2025 requests transparent reporting, including plan access, denominators, missing data and harms; a completed checklist is not a certificate of validity.

In a fictional study, a negative blood test is associated with favourable five-year outcomes while everyone receives standard treatment. Those data do not establish that stopping treatment after a negative result is safe. The missing question compares the proposed result-guided strategy with the relevant alternative, with matched sampling time, population, event, uncertainty and follow-up. Pretreatment, on-treatment and surgical samples describe different states. A later landmark includes only people eligible at that time and excludes earlier events; the last sample available during year one is not automatically an early postoperative sample. Analytical reliability, prognosis, treatment-effect prediction and benefit from a test-guided action require distinct evidence.
